title: Image-sensor correlated double sampling for bitline sensing
idea: Borrowed from CMOS image sensors: a switched-capacitor column comparator samples the bitline onto one small cap right after precharge (capturing kTC reset noise, random-telegraph noise and its own offset) and onto a second cap after the wordline opens, then decides on the difference. Everything common to both samples subtracts out.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): cuts required signal margin ~40-50%, so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF or bitlines can double in length (half the sense amps).

title: Avalanche-photodiode charge multiplier at the bitline foot
idea: Borrowed from avalanche photodiodes and photomultipliers: a gated impact-ionization junction at the sense node multiplies the few thousand electrons dumped by the cell 10-30x before the latch fires, the way an APD amplifies single photons. A ~1 ns bias pulse limits dark current to the sensing window.
why: Charge wall (facts 1-2): a 0.3-0.5 fF capacitor at AR ~15:1 gives today's signal, removing the 60-75:1 pillar etch and making stackable 3D capacitors viable.

title: Column-parallel single-slope ADC reads two bits per cell
idea: Borrowed from image-sensor column ADCs: one global voltage ramp is broadcast to all 8k columns of a mat, and each column's tiny comparator latches a shared Gray-code counter when the ramp crosses its bitline. Each cell stores four charge levels and is digitized in one ~8 ns ramp.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits/cell for ~15% extra periphery, because the per-column cost is one comparator plus two latches instead of three sense amps.

title: LIDAR time-to-digital converter turns bitline voltage into delay
idea: Borrowed from automotive LIDAR TDCs: the bitline voltage starves a short inverter chain so a 20 mV difference becomes ~30 ps of delay, and a digitally calibrated arbiter flip-flop decides the bit from arrival order. No large matched cross-coupled latch is needed.
why: Periphery area and voltage floor (facts 7, 10): sense-amp area down ~2x and sensing at 0.6 V, since time-domain resolution does not shrink with supply.

title: SerDes decision-feedback equalizer cancels bitline crosstalk
idea: Borrowed from high-speed SerDes DFE: sense amps fire in two staggered phases, and the decided values of phase-1 neighbors feed back through small programmed coupling capacitors to subtract their known crosstalk from phase-2 bitlines. Open-bitline arrays can then run at minimum pitch without dummy reference mats or twisting.
why: Density and periphery: removes the ~3-5% die area of edge dummy mats and lets bitline pitch tighten ~15% at the same F.

title: CCD bucket-brigade column shifts charge to one amplifier
idea: Borrowed from astronomical CCDs: in streaming banks, clocked gates along each column shift every cell's charge packet down to a single floating-diffusion source follower at the column end instead of dumping it onto a heavy bitline. The packet arrives undivided, so the signal is Cs/Cfd instead of Cs/Cbl.
why: Charge wall: signal gain ~20-50x versus charge sharing, permitting sub-fF cells; fits sequential AI weight streaming at ~1 ns per shift stage.

title: Laser-trimmed op-amp offset trim for minimum-size sense amps
idea: Borrowed from precision analog trimming: sense-amp transistors are drawn at minimum size (accepting large mismatch), and each SA gets a 3-bit trim capacitor array whose code is measured by power-up BIST and held in a small nonvolatile register per 8 SAs. Matching comes from digital trim instead of area.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~2.5-3x; stripes are ~10-15% of the die, so ~6-8% die per bit is saved.

title: LCD gate-on-array shift registers replace row decoders
idea: Borrowed from LCD gate-on-array scanning: rows in streaming banks are selected by a token passed down a compact shift register (one 4-6 transistor stage per wordline), exactly as panels scan gate lines. Random access stays in a smaller decoded side bank.
why: Periphery: row-decoder and predecode area down ~60-70% in banks serving sequential weight and KV-cache streams.

title: CDMA Walsh-coded wordlines read many gain cells at once
idea: Borrowed from cellular CDMA: N nondestructive gain cells on one bitline are activated together, each wordline modulated by an orthogonal Walsh code across N short read slots. One integrating sense block despreads the summed bitline current into N bits.
why: Periphery per bit: one sense block serves 8-16 cells per access with ~sqrt(N) noise processing gain, cutting sense amps ~4-8x in gain-cell arrays.

title: Resonant gate drive recovers wordline CV-squared energy
idea: Borrowed from resonant gate drivers in MHz power converters: groups of wordline drivers share an LC tank (inductor in the package or interposer), so each wordline charges along a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank on close instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of the ~3 V wordline swing energy and shrinks the VPP charge pump that feeds it.

title: Particle-detector zero suppression for sparse data bursts
idea: Borrowed from LHC detector readout zero suppression: each column group computes a wired-OR nonzero flag during sensing, and bytes that are all zero are sent as a 1-bit tag instead of toggling global data lines and I/O drivers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): AI activations and KV caches are 30-60% zero bytes, so global-bus and I/O energy drop ~25-45% for <1% area.

title: Hub-and-spoke periphery die time-shared by four array dies
idea: Borrowed from airline and parcel hub-and-spoke networks: four periphery-free array dies (cells and local latches only) stack on one logic-process hub die holding decoders, pumps, refresh, I/O and test, linked by hybrid bonds; the hub serves whichever array is active.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): amortizing periphery over four arrays lifts array efficiency from ~51% to ~80%+ and moves periphery to EUV-free mature logic.

title: EV battery-balancing capacitor ladder for stepwise bitline restore
idea: Borrowed from switched-capacitor active balancing in EV battery packs: bitlines are restored in three steps from a ladder of tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages, and on precharge they return charge down the same ladder instead of drawing everything from VDD.
why: Energy per bit (facts 8, 10): stepwise adiabatic charging cuts bitline restore energy ~2-3x, which matters most with 128x page overfetch.

title: Noise-cancelling headphone loop on the cell plate
idea: Borrowed from active noise cancellation and ECG driven-right-leg amplifiers: dummy bitlines in each mat pick up common-mode noise (plate bounce, wordline kick, substrate), and a fast amplifier drives the inverse onto the plate and reference lines during sensing.
why: Sensing margin: removes ~10-20 mV of correlated noise (~25% of today's budget), allowing smaller Cs or longer bitlines.

title: Smartphone pixel binning for leaky rows
idea: Borrowed from phone-camera pixel binning: when a retention monitor flags a weak row pair, the controller switches it to binned mode, where both cells hold the same bit and both wordlines open together to sum charge on the bitline; healthy rows stay at 1 bit per cell.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3): the <=13 fA tail cells stop setting the refresh rate, so the interval can stretch 4-8x for ~1-2% capacity.

title: RFID backscatter turns DRAM output into reflection
idea: Borrowed from passive RFID backscatter: the processor sends a continuous carrier down each data line, and the DRAM die only switches a small termination impedance to modulate the reflection, so it needs no output drivers or their supply current.
why: Data movement (fact 5): DRAM-side I/O energy down ~60-80% and I/O driver periphery shrinks; transmit power moves to the cheaper logic-node host.

title: Thermal circuit-breaker integrator tracks row hammer analogically
idea: Borrowed from bimetal thermal breakers: each wordline driver has a tiny leaky capacitor that gets a fixed charge quantum per activation and bleeds with a ~64 ms time constant; when a threshold comparator trips, it requests a neighbor refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~1k-activation thresholds with ~2 transistors and 1 capacitor per row instead of SRAM counter tables, ~0.5% area.

title: Pooled PCR group testing finds weak-retention cells in field
idea: Borrowed from Dorfman pooled testing: after an extended retention pause, the periphery merges many rows' compare results onto a wired-OR fail bus, flags pools with any failure, and bisects only failing pools; the results fill a per-row refresh-bin table.
why: Refresh (fact 3): cheap in-field profiling enables multi-rate refresh, cutting refresh energy ~50-70% for ~0.1% area.

title: Stacked image-sensor Cu-Cu bonding gives every bitline segment a sense amp
idea: Borrowed from Sony's pixel-parallel stacked image sensors: the array wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer at ~1 um pitch so each 32-64-cell bitline segment connects to its own sense amp below, eliminating long bitlines.
why: Charge wall: bitline capacitance drops ~10x, so ~0.5 fF or capacitorless cells work, and sense-amp stripes leave the array die (~15% area).

title: Core-memory coincident selection shrinks decoders and overfetch
idea: Borrowed from magnetic core memory's coincident-current addressing: each cell has two series access transistors, one gated by an X line and one by a Y line, so only the intersection is selected. A mat needs 2*sqrt(N) drivers, and one Y line opens just a 64-bit segment.
why: Periphery and overfetch (facts 7, 8): driver count per mat down ~30x and activation granularity ~128x finer, cutting random-read energy per useful bit ~5x.

title: Differential-GPS reference cells broadcast decay corrections
idea: Borrowed from differential GPS base stations: a few reference cells per mat, written at known levels, are sensed alongside each row to measure how much charge has leaked since refresh at the current temperature, and that correction trims the mat's shared sense reference.
why: Refresh (fact 3): sense amps correctly read half-decayed cells, stretching the refresh interval ~2x with negligible area.

title: CCFL piezoelectric transformer replaces wordline charge pumps
idea: Borrowed from the piezo transformers that drove LCD backlight lamps: an AlN bulk-acoustic resonator (the material of phone RF filters) steps a 1.1 V drive up to 3+ V at resonance, which is rectified into the wordline VPP rail.
why: Periphery and energy (facts 7, 10): charge pumps run ~30-40% efficient on ~2-4% of the die; piezo step-up targets ~70% efficiency in less area.

title: Flash translation layer remaps bad rows outside the die
idea: Borrowed from NAND SSD bad-block management: DRAM dies ship with no redundant rows, fuse banks or address comparators; the memory controller loads a per-die bad-row map from SPD and remaps addresses into a pooled spare region.
why: Periphery: deletes ~3-5% of die area (spares, fuses, compare logic) and pools spares across dies, raising effective yield.

title: AMOLED threshold-compensation sense amp on glass
idea: Borrowed from AMOLED 7T1C pixel compensation: in each IGZO or LTPS sense amp on a glass panel, the input transistors are first diode-connected so their own threshold is stored on a gate capacitor, then the bitline signal is applied on top, cancelling +/-300 mV thin-film threshold scatter.
why: Makes thin-film periphery on glass usable at ~30-50 mV margins, unlocking memory on Gen 8.5 panels (~60x a 300 mm wafer's area per substrate) with no EUV and no silicon.

title: X-ray flat-panel charge integrators read centimeter-long bitlines
idea: Borrowed from flat-panel X-ray detectors, which read ~1 fC pixel charges down 40 cm data lines: each glass-panel bitline is held at virtual ground by a switched-capacitor charge-integrating amplifier, so the cell's full charge transfers to a small feedback capacitor whatever the line capacitance.
why: Charge wall on glass: the signal is set by Cs/Cfb instead of Cs/Cbl, so bitlines can be ~10x longer and sense amps per bit fall ~10x.

title: Touchscreen mutual-capacitance sensing reads cells nondestructively
idea: Borrowed from projected-capacitive touch controllers: each cell is a coupling capacitor at a wordline-bitline crossing on glass whose value is shifted by a trapped-charge or ferroelectric layer; a TX pulse on the wordline and charge sensing on the bitline read it without discharging any storage node.
why: Destructive read (fact 8): no restore write-back on read and far less refresh, roughly halving read energy, built from thin films on any substrate.

title: MKID frequency multiplexing reads hundreds of segments per line
idea: Borrowed from astronomy's microwave kinetic inductance detector readout: on low-loss fused silica, each bitline segment gets a thin-film LC resonator at its own frequency whose Q is loaded by the selected cell's state, and one feedline carrying a frequency comb reads ~100-500 segments at once.
why: Periphery: one wideband receiver per feedline replaces hundreds of sense amps and column muxes; glass's low loss tangent makes inductors practical where silicon substrates kill Q.

title: LCD array-tester voltage imaging replaces on-die test periphery
idea: Borrowed from the LCD fab's electro-optic array tester, a modulator plate that images every pixel's voltage without contact: after the array layer on glass is built, a pattern is written and all cell voltages are imaged to find dead or weak-retention cells before periphery and stacking.
why: Periphery and capital: removes test-mode and BIST circuitry (~2-3% area) and probe cards, and yields full retention maps for refresh binning.

title: Panel laser-and-inkjet repair replaces fuse-based redundancy
idea: Borrowed from OLED and LCD line-repair stations: bitlines or wordlines found defective by in-line test are laser-cut and bridged to spare lines with inkjet-printed silver jumpers, so the glass memory needs no fuse banks or redundancy address comparators.
why: Periphery and yield: removes ~3% of area for redundancy logic and rescues large panel regions that a single defect would otherwise scrap.

title: MicroLED mass transfer of GaN-HEMT periphery chiplets onto glass
idea: Borrowed from microLED mass transfer: GaN HEMT sense-amp and driver chiplets (~50 um) are grown on sapphire, laser-lifted off and stamped thousands per second onto IGZO cell arrays on glass, then wired with panel metal.
why: Fast (2DEG mobility ~1500 cm2/Vs), high-voltage periphery with no silicon wafer, EUV or quartz crucible anywhere in the flow.

title: DWDM wavelength-addressed wordlines through transparent glass
idea: Borrowed from telecom DWDM: each wordline driver on a glass panel is a photo-TFT under a thin-film Fabry-Perot filter tuned to one of 64 wavelengths, and a fast tunable laser beneath the transparent substrate selects a row by color, with 1-of-16 electrical predecode choosing the mat.
why: Periphery: optical selection replaces row decoders and global address wiring, cutting decoder area ~70% in exchange for an off-panel photonic source.

title: Telephone-exchange relay logic rebuilt with NEMS relays on glass
idea: Borrowed from relay telephone exchanges, rebuilt with nano-electromechanical relays (metal beam, air gap) made on glass: decoder trees and mat power gates use relays with zero off-current, switched one cycle ahead because addresses arrive early.
why: Idle power: periphery standby leakage goes to ~0, and a relay process needs only metals and oxides, no silicon wafer.

title: OTDR reflectometry reads a whole column from one pulse
idea: Borrowed from optical time-domain reflectometers: a glass-panel bitline is built as a low-loss transmission line, each cell's state switches a small shunt impedance, and a ~20 ps pulse launched from one end returns reflections whose timing gives cell position and whose amplitude gives state.
why: Periphery: one fast receiver reads hundreds of cells per pulse instead of hundreds of sense amps; only practical on low-loss glass with centimeter lines.

title: LCD polarity inversion cancels oxide-TFT bias stress
idea: Borrowed from LCD dot inversion, which keeps liquid crystal from DC drift: the periphery stores each row inverted on alternate refresh epochs, tracked by a per-row polarity bit, so IGZO access and sense transistors see near-zero average bias stress.
why: Removes oxide-TFT threshold drift (often 100+ mV over life) from the sensing budget, so glass-panel sense amps can run tighter margins for longer.

title: LCD overdrive pre-emphasis speeds slow thin-film bitlines
idea: Borrowed from LCD response-time overdrive: column drivers apply a brief over-voltage pulse sized by a lookup table of previous and target state, so slow 20-40 cm2/Vs oxide-TFT bitlines and wordlines settle in about a third of the time.
why: Speed: moves glass-panel memory from ~100 ns toward ~30-40 ns cycles without high-mobility channels.

title: Ion-exchanged glass waveguides form the panel's global data bus
idea: Borrowed from ion-exchange waveguides used in planar fiber couplers: optical waveguides are written into the glass substrate itself, with microLED emitters at each mat and thin-film photodiodes at the panel edge replacing centimeter-long metal global I/O lines.
why: Data movement on large panels: long-wire CV2 energy becomes ~0.1-0.5 pJ/bit optical links, with no extra wiring layers since the waveguide is inside the substrate.

title: Qi-style inductive coupling stacks glass memory sheets without vias
idea: Borrowed from wireless charging and NFC coils: thin glass memory sheets are laminated with planar coils at each I/O site, passing data and clock inductively through glass, which unlike silicon has no eddy-current loss.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV or through-glass-via keep-out area or yield loss, and stacking is just lamination at ~1-2 pJ/bit per vertical link.

title: Downhole-oil-tool SiC electronics make refresh-free hot memory
idea: Borrowed from SiC electronics in oil-well logging tools and EV inverters: cells and CMOS periphery are built on 4H-SiC wafers (bandgap 3.26 eV), whose intrinsic carrier density is ~1e16x lower than silicon's, so junction leakage stays negligible at 150-200 C beside accelerators.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention of minutes to hours removes refresh engines and cooling needs, using U.S. SiC wafer capacity built for EVs.

title: Field-emission display tips become vacuum-channel sense amplifiers
idea: Borrowed from field-emission displays' nanogap emitters on glass: nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (sub-100 nm gaps, which work in air below the electron mean free path) serve as sense-amp input pairs whose transconductance does not depend on substrate crystal quality.
why: Gives glass substrates fast, high-gain sensing despite poor thin-film mobility, and is radiation-hard; a speculative path to periphery without silicon.

title: Display-fab turnkey lines for U.S. memory periphery
idea: Borrowed from the solar and display industries' turnkey-line model: buy standard Gen-6 glass toolsets (flat-panel i-line steppers, PECVD, sputter) and run memory panels with relaxed 1-2 um periphery rules, since glass area costs ~100x less than wafer area, sited in the U.S. within ~18-24 months.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: periphery capex per m2 ~10x below a DRAM fab, with no EUV and no quartz crucibles.

title: Mini-LVDS timing-controller links for on-panel data lines
idea: Borrowed from the reduced-swing differential links between TV timing controllers and source drivers: global data lines on a memory panel become current-mode differential pairs with ~200 mV swing, terminated at each mat cluster.
why: Energy per bit on long panel wires: ~5x lower than full-swing CMOS lines and tolerant of thin-film variation.

title: ARM-style IP licensing of thin-film periphery to display fabs
idea: Borrowed from ARM's licensing model: develop a validated library of oxide-TFT sense amps, decoders and pumps (with process recipes) and license it to underused Gen-6/8.5 display fabs for a royalty per square meter, so memory supply grows with existing panel capacity.
why: Supply and capital: taps tens of millions of m2 per year of display capacity without new fabs and turns periphery design into a reusable asset.

title: Foldable-phone flex hinge folds periphery behind the array
idea: Borrowed from foldable phones and flex-PCB folding: array and periphery are built side by side on polyimide, then the periphery strip is folded 180 degrees behind the array through a thin bent interconnect zone, so it takes no footprint and sits ~20 um under its mats.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): footprint array efficiency rises toward ~90% with short vertical links, without wafer bonding or TSVs.

title: Thin-film-solar steel foil acts as global plate and ground
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll CIGS solar on stainless-steel foil: oxide-TFT memory is built on insulated steel foil, and the foil itself, reached through periodic contacts, serves as cell plate, ground return and heat spreader.
why: Periphery: removes plate-line distribution and one or two power-mesh metal layers, and roll-to-roll processing cuts capital per m2.

title: Charlieplexed wordlines with thin-film bidirectional selectors
idea: Borrowed from LED charlieplexing: wordlines are selected by ordered pairs of N driver lines through back-to-back oxide Schottky-diode selectors on glass, so N drivers address N(N-1) rows (32 drivers select 992 rows).
why: Periphery: row-driver count per mat down ~30x, which matters on glass where thin-film drivers are large.

title: Event-camera address-event bus for self-requested refresh
idea: Borrowed from neuromorphic event cameras' address-event representation: each row on a glass panel has a sentinel cell with a deliberately weaker capacitor and a thin-film comparator that fires the row address onto an arbitrated event bus when it decays, so only rows that need refresh get it.
why: Refresh (fact 3): oxide-TFT cells rarely leak, so event-driven refresh cuts refresh operations 100x+ versus timed sweeps and removes the refresh counter.
